tier_reason: Upgraded B to A. The VLDB'18 paper (Sec. 6) states the CPU (AMD Ryzen Threadripper 1950X fixed at 3.4 GHz), the compiler (g++ 5.4.0-6) and the flags (-Ofast -march=native). The benchmark code is public in the repo: benchmarking/benchmark_mf.cc and benchmarking/benchmark_cf.cc, whose Makefile clones Fan et al.'s efficient/cuckoofilter at a pinned commit and patches it for the head-to-head baseline.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Paper vs Fan et al.'s reference cuckoo filter (CF): lookups 1.3x-2.5x faster (1.3x-2.5x for true negatives, Fig. 11; 1.6x-2.4x for true positives, Fig. 10), insertions 0.9x-15.5x (Fig. 12), deletions 1.3x-1.6x (Fig. 13). The README's 'up to 15.5x, 1.3x, and 2.5x' understates deletion; the paper says up to 1.6x. The MF uses about 11.71 bits/item at 0.95 load vs a 12-bit-fingerprint CF. The paper does not benchmark Bloom filters. Its point about using fewer bits than a Bloom filter below ~1-3% FPR is a general statement about cuckoo/quotient filters.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: g++ 5.4.0-6 with -Ofast -march=native (paper Sec. 6). The repo benchmarking/Makefile uses -Ofast -march=native -mpopcnt -std=c++11. The README recommends g++ 5.4 and reports a GCC 8.x performance regression as of March 2019.
corrections.hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper 1950X (2x8 cores, 32 MB L3), frequency fixed at 3400 MHz, 128 GB DDR4-2133, Ubuntu 16.04.4 LTS (Linux 4.11.0)
corrections.workload: Fan et al.'s reference cuckoo filter (plus semi-sorted CF and RSQF) vs a Morton filter with 128*1024*1024 slots and 8-bit fingerprints (3-slot buckets). The filters are filled to each load factor in steps of 0.05. Then 0.1% of total slots are inserted, deleted or looked up with 64-bit random keys. Results are the average of 5 trials (VLDB 2018 paper).
corrections.caveats: The README says this is an academic prototype. The batch API works correctly only when the input is a multiple of 128. A later deletion correctness fix cut peak deletion throughput from about 38 to about 28 MOPS, so current code may not reproduce the paper's deletion numbers. Insertion speedup is 0.9x (slower) at some load factors. The repo has no commits since 2020-12-16.

notes: The paper's methodology is complete and the benchmark harness is in the repo, so the tier is upgraded to A. claimed_speedup is corrected to the paper's ranges. The README's deletion figure (1.3x) is the low end of the paper's 1.3x-1.6x. Metadata checks out: MIT license, 90 stars, last commit 2020-12-16, abandoned, not a fork.

tier_reason: The peer-reviewed SIGMOD'18 paper compares RocksDB using SuRF against RocksDB's Bloom filters at equal memory (14 bits/key) on an i7-6770HQ. The code is public: bench/ in the repo and the efficient/rocksdb fork. The paper states no compiler name or version, so the entry cannot be tier A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: RocksDB with SuRF vs RocksDB's Bloom filter at equal filter size: open-range (Open-Seek) queries 1.5x faster, and closed-range queries up to 5x faster (SuRF-Real, when 99% of queries return empty). On the worst-case all-miss point-query workload, the abstract says RocksDB is up to 40% slower with SuRF because of a higher false-positive rate (0.2% vs 0.1%). Fig. 12 point throughput is 32.9 Kops/s for Bloom, 19.8 for SuRF-Hash and 16.4 for SuRF-Real. So SuRF-Real is about 50% slower (derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. The SuRF repo's CMake Release flags are -O3 -Wall -Werror -mpopcnt -pthread -std=c++11, with the compiler unspecified. The RocksDB end-to-end runs used the efficient/rocksdb fork, whose build flags were not checked.
corrections.caveats: This is a mixed result, not a strict win. SuRF is 40-50% slower for all-miss point queries at equal filter size, and the paper says adding a few suffix bits per key closes the gap. Its wins (1.5x-5x) are for range queries only. The paper reports throughput in Kops/s, not latency. The end-to-end code lives in the efficient/rocksdb fork (last push 2018-12-20). The microbenchmarks (bench/workload.cpp vs bench/filter_bloom.hpp) ran on a Xeon E5-2680 v2. The GitHub license API says NOASSERTION, but the LICENSE file is the plain Apache-2.0 text. bench/bloom.hpp is LevelDB-derived code under a BSD-style license.

notes: The numbers match the abstract and Sec. 6. Fig. 12 shows SuRF-Real's point-query penalty is about 50%, larger than the abstract's 40%, so this was added. The record's metric 'latency' is wrong: the paper measures throughput and I/Os per operation. The metric field is not correctable here. Metadata checks out: Apache-2.0, 554 stars, last commit 2022-03-11, abandoned.

tier_reason: The peer-reviewed PVLDB 13 paper compares vacuum filters against Bloom, blocked Bloom, cuckoo, Morton and CQF filters on a stated Intel E5-2687W CPU. It gives no compiler or flags. The repo has only a demo (test.cpp), not the comparison harness, so the entry cannot be tier A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Abstract: about 25% less space on average and similar throughput vs cuckoo filters, and about 15% less space and >10x throughput vs Bloom filters, at the same false-positive rate. In memory: VF-ss is about 1.1x-1.8x faster than CF-ss for positive lookups. VFs have the highest lookup throughput below 90% occupancy, but CFs are slightly better at high occupancy. VFs have the highest insertion throughput below 65% occupancy, and deletion throughput is similar to CFs. On SSD with a 100 MB memory limit, VF lookups are 1.86x-2.13x faster than CF. Space: VFs save 2-5 bits per item vs the other methods in the average case (about 5 fewer bits vs CFs).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. The repo makefile builds the test.cpp demo with g++ -Ofast -march=native -mpopcnt -std=c++14 (plus -pg -g).
corrections.caveats: The paper gives the CPU but no compiler or flags. The repo has no harness for the Bloom, Morton and CQF comparisons, only the test.cpp demo and Fan et al.'s inherited CF benchmarks under ModifiedCuckooFilter/. The top-level license is MIT, added 2024-11-23. ModifiedCuckooFilter/ is Apache-2.0 code derived from CMU/Intel's cuckoofilter. The throughput advantage over cuckoo filters is small or reversed at high occupancy.

notes: The numbers match Sec. 6.2. The abstract's '>10x throughput vs Bloom filters' headline was added. The '2-5 fewer bits' claim is scoped to the paper's average case. Metadata checks out: MIT (plus an Apache-2.0 subdirectory), 54 stars, last commit 2024-11-23, stale.
